sources.news_title: Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after four decades
sources.text:
Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after four decades
WASHINGTON — Christiane Amanpour, CNN's chief international anchor, said on Monday that she will leave the news network next June after 43 years, according to an internal memo on Monday.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said in a statement.
Amanpour, 68, said she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour, a household name worldwide for her heroism as a foreign correspondent, has hosted an eponymous nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009.
In January 2025, she scaled back to hosting a few days a week. In January 2027, she will shift the program to once a week, until it ends in May. She will continue reporting and traveling the world for CNN through June.
CNN chairman Mark Thompson shared Amanpour’s decision in a memo to colleagues Monday morning.
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”
Thompson described her as “one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere” and said the network will take time to celebrate her “before she departs next year.”
“In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship,” he wrote.
In her statement, Amanpour said she wanted to thank “all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews.”
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much,” she said, “as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.”
Amanpour’s PBS iteration, “Amanpour & Company,” will end in December.
In her statement, Amanpour said she will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with ex-husband Jamie Rubin, produced by Global.

sources.news_title: It’s hard not to read into Christiane Amanpour’s CNN exit
sources.text:
Legendary anchor and foreign correspondent Christiane Amanpour announced Monday that she would leave CNN next year after more than four decades at the cable network.
“After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless nights, as you can imagine, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years,” she said.
Amanpour, the network’s chief international anchor, said in a statement that she’ll leave next June and that she “looks forward to interesting new projects down the line.” She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with ex-husband Jamie Rubin.
Amanpour’s departure would be notable under any circumstances. She joined CNN as an assistant on its international assignment desk in 1983, when the network was just 3 years old, and became one of the journalists who defined its identity around the world. Her reporting from the Gulf War, Bosnia, Rwanda, Afghanistan and other conflicts helped establish CNN as a global news organization.
But the timing of her announcement makes it even more significant. Amanpour will be the first major CNN personality to announce her departure since David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance acquired CNN parent company Warner Bros. Discovery earlier this month, bringing CNN and CBS News under the same owner.
There is no indication that Ellison’s takeover prompted Amanpour’s decision. CNN CEO Mark Thompson said Monday that he and Amanpour had been discussing her departure “for some months.”
Still, Amanpour has made clear that she has concerns about the new ownership.
In May, before the deal was completed, Amanpour criticized what she called the “ideological realignment of CBS and the destruction, potentially, of ‘60 Minutes’” and said she was “concerned.” Her comments came after Paramount Skydance installed Bari Weiss as editor-in-chief of CBS News. Weiss, who had no television news experience and was best known for her contrarian commentary at The New York Times before launching The Free Press, quickly began reshaping the network.
Those changes led to the departures or firings of a number of longtime CBS News staff members, most notably at “60 Minutes.” Among them was Anderson Cooper, who worked as a “60 Minutes” correspondent for more than 20 years before departing the program in July. Notably, Cooper, who remains one of CNN’s biggest stars, signed a contract extension with CNN in December.
Amanpour didn’t directly reference Ellison or the deal in her departure, but she did nod to journalistic independence several times.
“You know that I’ve always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you for as long as I am here and beyond,” she said. “That’s especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides — political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field.”

She also said she “will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism.”
CNN will enter its Ellison era with more continuity at the top than its new sister news network at CBS. Shortly before the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery deal closed, the company announced that Thompson would remain chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN. Ellison has also pledged to preserve CNN’s editorial independence, and Skydance agreed as part of a settlement with states that challenged the merger to establish an independent board of journalists charged with safeguarding the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News.
But that won’t stop people from reading into Amanpour’s departure. CNN is losing a journalist who has been around almost as long as the cable network has existed. It’s also losing a journalist who has made independence a defining part of her public identity.
Viewers and fans have plenty of time to catch Amanpour before she departs. Her CNN International program will scale back to once a week at the beginning of 2027 before ending in May. Her PBS program, “Amanpour & Company,” will end in December.
And in June, she’ll formally leave CNN, 43 years after arriving as an entry-level assistant.
By Ren LaForme, managing editor
Jon Stewart isn’t going anywhere
Jon Stewart also had a major announcement Monday: He’ll stick around at “The Daily Show” through the 2028 election.
Stewart returned to the Comedy Central show in February 2024 after nine years away. Though he only hosts on Mondays, his return has been a boost for the show, which recently posted its best third-quarter audience in eight years. Comedy Central said “The Daily Show” has also racked up 1.6 billion views across social media this year.
Stewart’s announcement is notable for a couple of reasons.
First, Comedy Central is now part of the new Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery megacompany, known simply as Skydance. Stewart has been a frequent and sharp critic of President Donald Trump, conservative media and, increasingly, his own corporate bosses.
After CBS announced last year that it would cancel “The Late Show with Stephen Colbert,” Stewart openly questioned Paramount’s explanation that the decision was purely financial. The cancellation came as Paramount was seeking government approval for its merger with Skydance, and shortly after the company agreed to pay $16 million to settle Trump’s lawsuit over a “60 Minutes” interview.
Stewart also wondered aloud about his own future. His contract was set to expire at the end of this year, and the uncertainty continued for months even as Paramount said it wanted him to stay.
The renewal is also notable because it runs against the prevailing winds in late-night TV. CBS aired the final episode of “The Late Show” in May, ending a franchise that had been on the air for 33 years. ABC’s future in the space is uncertain as Disney negotiates with Jimmy Kimmel over a new contract. Disney President Dana Walden recently called late night a “very challenging day part.”
By Ren LaForme, managing editor

sources.news_title: The truth behind Christiane Amanpour’s exit as CNN execs begged her to stay
sources.text:
Legendary host and reporter Christiane Amanpour announced she was leaving CNN on Monday, not long after David and Larry Ellison made their ownership official.
The Ellisons' purchase of CBS in Aug. 2025 ushered in the network's lack of independence on the news side, insiders have said over the past year. Less than 24 hours before Amanpour's announcement, Semafor reported that editor-in-chief Bari Weiss had CBS News reporters chasing conspiracy theories that Texas Democrat James Talarico was in a mental health facility in Ohio, among others.
What has happened at CBS News over the past year appears to have helped with Amanpour's decision to leave.
According to Oliver Darcy's "Status," Amanpour convened a meeting on Monday morning with her team and by 11 a.m., CNN chief Mark Thompson was sending a memo to the full network announcing she was leaving.
"After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter," Thompson wrote. "Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, Amanpour, to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June."
Darcy explained that many CNN contracts expire in 2027, but Amanpour's public exit as the first doesn't bode well for the network's future.
The Daily Beast said that Thompson "personally begged" the reporter not to leave. Meanwhile, he also launched "a quiet, unsuccessful campaign to stop their premier international anchor from walking out the door." However, she had her own concerns about the news network under the new owners.
Darcy also learned that the journalist's health somewhat influenced her decision. The two-time cancer survivor revealed that her ovarian cancer returned for the third time, though she assured it was "being very well managed." But Amanpour decided it was time to move on anyway.
Thompson confessed in his message that he'd been trying to persuade her to stay for months, to no avail.
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote.
She, like many, is concerned that the Ellisons' acquisition of the network could shift the news networks away from fact-based reporting and more toward support for President Donald Trump and other Republicans.
When reporters told him on October 6, 2026, that the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger had closed, Trump cheered, “I’m happy about that. That’s great. It’s gonna be a great company. They’re terrific people, and it’s gonna be a great company.”
“That’s a great merger. I’m glad they let it go," he added.
Trump has long opposed CNN, claiming that the network is spreading “poison and lies." The network is one of three that Trump has attempted to remove from the White House. In fact, this year marked the second attempt Trump made to remove CNN, the first being with reporter Jim Acosta during his first term.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth similarly cheered, “The sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.”

sources.text:
Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour, who began as an entry-level assistant and rose to become one of the most visible correspondents and anchors on TV, reporting from war zones and hot spots for decades, will be leaving the network after 43 years.
Amanpour, the network’s chief international anchor, will scale back her daily show, “Amanpour,” on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end it in May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement Monday that she looks forward to “interesting new projects down the line.”
Watch NBC 5 free wherever you are
Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, “Amanpour & Co,” at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” Amanpour said. She added she would “always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: Always be truthful, not neutral.”

No reason given for her departure
Amanpour did not give a reason for her departure, nor did she specifically mention changes at her network. But her exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN.
On a personal front, Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and two later recurrences, calling it “the invisible killer.” She has urged others to “get all the scans that you can.”
U.S. & World
Amanpour joined CNN as an assistant in Atlanta in 1983. In his own message Monday, CNN's chief executive, Mark Thompson, wrote that at the time, her promise was not universally appreciated. “Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent — or to hold any on-air role at all,” Thompson wrote. “Boy, did she prove him wrong!”
Fame came during the first Gulf War
Amanpour became a reporter and an international correspondent seven years later. She earned fame in the early 1990s, covering the Gulf War, conflict in the Middle East and many other hot spots. War reporting is “a sense of mission, it’s a sense of purpose, it’s a sense of being able to tell a story,” she said.
She aimed to bring international news — including complicated stories — to American viewers. “I’ve never believed that things are too complicated to put on American television,” she told The Associated Press in 2023. "I’ve never talked down to an audience. I’ve never believed that they just want to know what’s happening in their backyard.”
Amanpour also noted that her upbringing gave her a unique perspective.
“Because of my upbringing — I’m half-Iranian and half-British — I’ve had the great privilege of being able to see the world from two very distinct perspectives,” she said. “I’ve always spoken out about the need to bridge gaps. I know we can live in a world that’s not 100% tribalized.”
In her remarks Monday, Amanpour thanked her field crews and show teams.
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much,” she wrote, “as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.”

sources.text:
Christiane Amanpour announces departure from CNN
CNN's chief international anchor Christiane Amanpour is leaving the US TV network.
London-born Amanpour, 68, who has become a household name worldwide as a foreign correspondent, will be signing off in June.
Amanpour - who has hosted a nightly interview program on CNN International since 2009 - told viewers of her decision on Monday.
"After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless lights, as you can imagine, I've decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years - longer than many marriages.
"So this daily show on CNN and PBS will come to an end at the end of this year but CNN and I have worked out a smooth transition while continuing doing Amanpour once a week through to June."
CNN chairman Mark Thompson described her as "one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere".
"Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months," he said in a memo to colleagues.
"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally."
He thanked her for "43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship".
In January 2025, she scaled back to hosting a few days a week.
From January 2027, the program will shift to once a week, until it ends in May, CNN said.
She will continue reporting and travelling the world for CNN through to June.
Amanpour thanked "all the amazingly talented people I've worked with throughout this incredible journey," especially her show teams and field crews.
"From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf war, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much," she said.
"As we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favour".
She was made a CBE "for services to journalism" by Queen Elizabeth II in 2007.

Veteran CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour announces exit from network, will go off the air next June
Veteran CNN International anchor Christiane Amanpour announced Monday she’s leaving the network next summer after more than four decades at the network.
“After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter,” CNN CEO Mark Thompson told staffers in a memo. “Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, ‘Amanpour,’ to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June.”
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally,” Thompson wrote.
Amanpour thanked her viewers and alluded to the “pressures” she and her CNN colleagues face during an on-air address.
“Now, you know I’ve always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you for as long as I am here and beyond,” Amanpour said. “That’s especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides, political, financial and also from the rising dangers in the field. I’ll always be rooting for CNN maintaining its history of independent journalism.”
“Remember: always be truthful, not neutral,” she also said in a written statement.
The announcement came as a shock to CNN staffers. One called her CNN’s “reigning titan.” Another described themselves as a “Christiane loyalist” and called her “the heart and soul of this company,” but admitted her stature in journalism can continue without CNN.
“She has the power to chart her own course. Yes, she is synonymous with a brand, but she is also a bigger than the brand,” the CNN staffer told Fox News Digital.
While the 68-year-old journalist is revered among her CNN colleagues and members of the liberal media, she has her critics as well. As she referenced in her statement, Amanpour rejects the notion of neutrality when it comes to reporting, insisting the truth should remain the north star.
“Both-siderism — on the one hand, on the other hand — is not always objectivity. It does not get you to the truth,” Amanpour told graduates at the Columbia Journalism School in 2023. “Drawing false, moral or factual equivalence is neither objective or truthful. Objectivity is our golden rule. And it is in weighing all the sides and all the evidence hearing everyone reporting everything, but not rushing to equate them when there is no equating and look at the damage that that has done in the climate debate, in the political arena and in the field of battle.”
CNN’S CHRISTIANE AMANPOUR CALLS OUT BOSS CHRIS LICHT, OFFERS STUNNING REBUKE OF TRUMP TOWN HALL
Her coverage of the Israel-Hamas war and her past commentary have also raised eyebrows. Amanpour claimed in October 2023, just weeks after the terrorist attack on Israel, “the rest of the world” agreed with Jordanian Queen Rania Al Abdullah’s complaint that the Western world shows more support for Israel than the Palestinians. She also reported that third-party negotiators were trying to implement a “hostage release on both sides,” implying Israel, too, is keeping civilian hostages and not just the Hamas terrorists. Earlier in the year, she was forced to apologize after she claimed the murder of an Israeli rabbi’s family was the result of a “shootout.”
In November 2020, she was condemned by the Israeli government and the Anti-Defamation League for comparing the Trump presidency to Kristallnacht, known as the “Night of Broken Glass” when Nazis terrorized Jews throughout Germany and Austria, resulting in at least 91 deaths and 7,500 Jewish businesses vandalized during the Holocaust. Amanpour walked back her comments following the intense backlash.
Amanpour’s forthcoming exit from CNN marks the first major journalist set to leave the network under its new corporate ownership. Skydance CEO and Paramount owner David Ellison recently closed on his $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, merging two legacy Hollywood studios as well as several television networks including CNN and CBS under Skydance.
While there’s been no indication her decision was tied to Ellison’s takeover of the network, Amanpour isn’t shy to publicly challenge her bosses, most notably Thompson’s predecessor Chris Licht, for airing the now-infamous Trump town hall in 2023. Earlier this year, Amanpour expressed concern about Ellison owning CNN over how he’s handled CBS News since he bought Paramount and installed Bari Weiss as its editor-in-chief.
“I’m concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that he’s taken over already, like CBS News, right?” Amanpour said in May. “I mean, do I have to list what’s happening there? I mean, hemorrhaging viewers, probably hemorrhaging money, this ideological realignment of CBS and the destruction, potentially, of ‘60 Minutes.’”

Longtime CNN anchor Christiane Amanpour, who began as an entry-level assistant and rose to become one of the most visible correspondents and anchors on TV, reporting from war zones and hot spots for decades, will be leaving the network after 43 years.
Amanpour, the network’s chief international anchor, will scale back her daily show, “Amanpour,” on CNN International to once a week at the beginning of 2027, and end it in May, leaving the network the following month. She said in a statement Monday that she looks forward to “interesting new projects down the line.”
Amanpour, 68, also will end her PBS show, “Amanpour & Co,” at the end of the year, she said in her statement, shared by CNN. She will continue her podcast, “The Ex Files,” with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat.

Amanpour did not give a reason for her departure, nor did she specifically mention changes at her network. But her exit coincides with a new era at CNN as it comes under a new owner, Skydance. After a yearlong process, Skydance-owned Paramount closed its $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. The merger unites under one roof two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN.
On a personal front, Amanpour has spoken openly about her 2021 diagnosis of ovarian cancer and two later recurrences, calling it “the invisible killer.” She has urged others to “get all the scans that you can.”
Amanpour joined CNN as an assistant in Atlanta in 1983. Amanpour's daily programs will end at the close of 2026. Beginning in January, her CNN International program will shift to once a week and then conclude in May.
Her PBS program, Amanpour & Company, will also end in December, while she has said she will continue The Ex Files, the podcast she hosts with former husband James Rubin.
Her coming departure provides a natural endpoint from which to look back at the assignments that turned an entry-level CNN employee into the network's chief international anchor.
Bosnia and Sarajevo Defined Amanpour's Approach to War Reporting
If the Gulf War established Amanpour's reputation, the war in Bosnia helped define the journalism philosophy she became associated with.
Amanpour reported extensively from the conflict and the siege of Sarajevo. During the war, she also interviewed Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladić, who was later convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Her reporting from Bosnia made her prominent beyond CNN, but it also sparked debate over whether her coverage crossed the line from objectivity into advocacy.
Amanpour rejected the idea that objectivity required journalists to create equivalence between opposing claims regardless of the underlying evidence. Her response to criticism of her Bosnia coverage became central to her broader argument about journalism: reporters should give competing sides a hearing but should not treat demonstrably unequal circumstances as equal merely in the name of neutrality.
That philosophy remains part of her public identity decades later. In Monday's announcement, Amanpour distilled it into a message about being "truthful, not neutral."
Reporting on Rwanda and the World's Humanitarian Crises
Amanpour's work during the 1990s went well beyond Bosnia. She reported from Rwanda and subsequently covered conflicts and humanitarian crises across Africa, Asia and the Middle East, assignments that helped establish foreign reporting as the through line of her career.
She specifically included Rwanda among the places she remembered when announcing her departure, grouping it with Bosnia, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran as assignments where she and her colleagues tried to document the evidence and human consequences of global conflict.
By then, her role inside CNN had expanded substantially. Amanpour served as the network's chief international correspondent from 1992 to 2010, during which her assignments included Iraq, Afghanistan, Iran, Israel, Pakistan, Somalia, Rwanda, and the Balkans.
Her work also crossed network boundaries. Beginning in the 1990s, she contributed international reports to 60 Minutes while continuing her work for CNN.
Afghanistan and the Post-9/11 Era
The September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks ushered in another period in which Amanpour's international experience put her at the center of CNN's coverage. Afghanistan became another conflict she later singled out as a defining assignment.
After the attacks, she secured interviews with major leaders confronting the emerging international crisis, including British Prime Minister Tony Blair, French President Jacques Chirac, and Pakistani President Pervez Musharraf.
Her reporting placed her at the intersection of battlefield coverage and the diplomacy surrounding the wars that followed 9/11.
Afghanistan also demonstrated the longevity of a career that had already spanned conflicts on several continents. Rather than leaving war reporting behind as she became more established on television, Amanpour continued returning to major international crises while simultaneously becoming one of CNN's principal interviewers.
Amanpour's Interviews With Presidents, Dictators and Global Leaders
Amanpour's career eventually became defined as much by the people sitting across from her as by the conflicts she covered in the field.
Over the decades, she interviewed an unusually broad range of political leaders, including Iranian Presidents Mohammad Khatami, Hassan Rouhani, and Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, as well as Musharraf, former Prime Minister of Zimbabwe Robert Mugabe, former Prime Minister of Libya Muammar Gaddafi, French President Emmanuel Macron and former Chancellor of Germany Angela Merkel. Other high-profile interviewees included Hillary Clinton, John Kerry and the Dalai Lama.
In February 2011, while working for ABC News, Amanpour interviewed Gaddafi and his sons amid the uprising against his government. The interview fell during her brief period away from CNN after she left the network in 2010 to anchor This Week.
She returned to CNN International in 2012 under an arrangement that initially allowed her to retain a role with ABC. Her interview program Amanpour became the central platform for the next phase of her career.
The Iran Interview Amanpour Walked Away From
One of Amanpour's most widely discussed interviews in recent years never happened.
In September 2022, she was scheduled to interview the late Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi in New York during the United Nations General Assembly. Raisi's team canceled the interview after requesting that Amanpour wear a headscarf during the appearance, according to accounts of the episode.
Amanpour, who is Iranian-British and spent part of her childhood in Tehran, refused. She later said that despite interviewing Iranian presidents since the 1990s, no one had ever asked her to cover her hair when interviewing someone outside Iran.
The episode came as protests were unfolding in Iran following the death of Mahsa Amini, making the disagreement over the interview's conditions particularly consequential.
CNN's Skydance Takeover and the Ellisons' Trump Relationship
Amanpour's announcement comes less than two weeks after one of the biggest corporate changes in CNN's history.
On October 6, Skydance-owned Paramount completed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, bringing CNN and CBS News under the same corporate owner. Including debt, the acquisition amounted to nearly $111 billion. The combined company, known as Skydance, is led by billionaire David Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz.
The newsroom implications have attracted particular scrutiny because of the Ellison family's relationship with President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly attacked CNN over its coverage. The Associated Press reported that the Ellison family has long supported Trump, and Larry Ellison, David Ellison's father and co-founder of Oracle, has financially supported him. Trump welcomed the completed merger this month, saying Skydance was "going to be a great company."
David Ellison has pledged to preserve editorial independence. A settlement reached with states that challenged the merger also requires Skydance to create a board to oversee editorial independence at CNN and CBS News, while Thompson remains in charge of CNN's news operation.
The takeover's proximity to Amanpour's announcement is notable, but no evidence has been reported so far that the change in ownership prompted her decision.
When she finally signs off next June, she will leave amid another transformation, this time not on a battlefield overseas but inside the company where her career began.

Longtime international correspondent Christiane Amanpour will exit CNN in June
LOS ANGELES – Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s chief international anchor whose intrepid reporting became a symbol of the network’s global reach and influence, announced Monday she will end her 43-year run in June.
Amanpour, 68, told colleagues in a memo she will step away from her eponymous daily CNN program at the end of the year. She will continue her Saturday program, “The Amanpour Hour,” until May before exiting the following month.
Amanpour was one of CNN’s first breakout stars, traveling the world to report on global hot spots and helping build CNN’s strong reputation for international coverage, especially in war zones. She was front and center as the network delivered images of the first Gulf war, the Bosnian war and conflicts in Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran.
Amanpour’s announcement arrives as CNN faces uncertainty under new ownership. Skydance absorbed the network as part of its $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. International bureaus are expected to be the first place where CNN and Skydance’s CBS News are expected to consolidate resources. Deliberations over editorial direction are likely to be intense.
There have been reports of internal strife at the London bureau at CBS News over the tone of its Middle East coverage since Bari Weiss, a strong supporter of Israel, took over as the network’s editor in chief last year. Weiss replaced Claire Day, a longtime veteran of the network, with Shayndi Rice, a former Wall Street Journal editor overseeing all of the network’s international operations.
In a memo to staff obtained by The Times, CNN Worldwide Chairman and Chief Executive Mark Thompson said he has discussed Amanpour’s future for several months. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally,” he wrote.
Amanpour did not offer a reason for her departure, devoting most of her memo to thanking the production crews who worked with her over the years. She said she will continue to co-host “The Ex-Files,” a podcast she co-hosts with her ex-husband Jamie Rubin, a former journalist who served in the State Department during the Clinton administration.
Amanpour was born and raised in Tehran, Iran. Her family fled the country in 1979 during the Islamic Revolution. She arrived at CNN in 1983, working as a news desk assistant in Atlanta and then at its New Your bureau with the ambition of becoming a foreign correspondent.
Amanpour’s reporting from war zones and ability to land interviews with global leaders made her one of the most recognizable journalists in the world. During her time at CNN, she served as a contributor to the CBS newsmagazine “60 Minutes.” She also served as anchor of the ABC News Washington roundtable program “This Week” from Aug. 2010 to Dec. 2011.
Amanpour’s work has been recognized with 16 News and Documentary Emmy Awards, four Peabody Awards, two George Polk Awards and three duPont-Columbia Awards.

In 2010, Amanpour temporarily left CNN to become the anchor of ABC News’ Sunday public affairs program “This Week,” succeeding George Stephanopoulos. She subsequently returned to CNN, where she continued reporting and hosting international news programming.

sources.news_title: Amanpour Announces Plan To Quit CNN After 43 Years
sources.text:
- CNN anBy Enyichukwu Enemannacnn
Veteran broadcast journalist, Christiane Amanpour has announced plans to leave CNN in June 2027, ending a 43-year career with the global news network.
Amanpour, 68, announced her decision on Monday, saying she had spent months considering her future before deciding to part ways with the broadcaster.
“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” she said in a statement.
She expressed hope of pursuing new opportunities after her departure while reaffirming her support for the network’s journalism.
“I look forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism,” she said.
Amanpour added, “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
CNN chairman Mark Thompson confirmed the decision in a memo to staff, saying he and Amanpour had been discussing it for several months.
“Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally,” Thompson said.
Amanpour joined CNN in the early 1980s, initially working as a news assistant before becoming one of its most prominent international correspondents.
Over the course of her career, she reported on major global conflicts, including the Gulf War, the Bosnian War and the genocide in Rwanda. Her assignments also took her to Afghanistan, Iraq, Ukraine and Iran.
She has interviewed world leaders and reported on major political and humanitarian developments, establishing a reputation for international reporting and challenging interviews.
Amanpour has hosted CNN’s international interview programme, Amanpour, since 2009. The programme is expected to move to a weekly schedule in January before ending in May 2027, while she continues reporting and travelling on assignments for CNN until June.
Her public television programme, Amanpour & Company, which airs on PBS in the United States, is also scheduled to end in December 2026.
Amanpour briefly left CNN in 2010 to become the anchor of ABC News’ This Week, succeeding George Stephanopoulos, before returning to the network.

Christiane Amanpour Will Leave CNN in June After 43 Years

Christiane Amanpour Will Leave CNN in June After 43 Years
Christiane Amanpour, CNN's chief international anchor, plans to leave the network at the end of June 2027, NBC News reported on Monday. CNN chief executive Mark Thompson announced the departure in a letter to newsroom employees that NBC obtained.
Amanpour, 68, joined CNN in 1983. The Hollywood Reporter said she will end her daily programs across CNN and PBS when this year closes.
Schedule for the Exit
Her program on CNN International will shrink to a weekly broadcast early in 2027, according to Thompson's letter as described by NBC News. That show will conclude in May. Amanpour will then spend June helping with the handover before she departs.
She will keep hosting her podcast, The Ex Filed, with her ex-husband Jamie Rubin, a former U.S. diplomat and Assistant Secretary of State. CNN does not produce the podcast, The Hollywood Reporter said.
What Thompson and Amanpour Said
Thompson wrote that Amanpour had considered the decision carefully and that the two had discussed it for some months. He said he was sorry to see her go but had accepted that the timing suited her personally and professionally.
Amanpour said in a statement, as reported by The Hollywood Reporter, that she made the choice after many months of thought and some sleepless nights. She thanked her show teams and field crews.
NBC News quoted her as saying she and her colleagues had worked to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity so that CNN could report the truth without fear or favor.
Ownership Change at CNN
Amanpour has not said why she is leaving, and The Hollywood Reporter said the reason is unclear. The announcement comes weeks after Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which brought CNN under its ownership.
At an event in May, Amanpour said she was concerned about the takeover, pointing to what had happened at CBS News after David Ellison's company took it over.
Thompson will continue to lead CNN for now, The Hollywood Reporter said, though it described the longer term as open.
Four Decades of Coverage
NBC News listed the major events Amanpour has covered, including the fall of the Berlin Wall, the Bosnian War and the Persian Gulf War.
Her reporting also took in the U.S. wars in Iraq and Afghanistan after the Sept. 11 attacks, the Arab Spring, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and Israel's war in Gaza.
Her interview subjects have included former President Bill Clinton, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair and Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi. She has also interviewed Iranian presidents Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and Hassan Rouhani.
